newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Solomon Burke administers some old-time soul.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Solomon Burke administers some old-time soul.

text.p: In a pristine church at odds with the seamy downtown Los Angeles neighbourhood in which it stands, a portly preacher is holding court on a recent Saturday night.

During his hour-long sermon, Bishop Burke sings such gospel standards as "Peace in the Valley" and "Crying in the Chapel" and delivers some spine-tingling oratory. "When you give yourself to Jesus something special happens," he booms as the pianist punctuates his remarks. "If you want God to touch you right now, get on your feet right now, and I dare you to touch God!"

The congregation responds with delirous shrieks and applause. When everyone has reached a state of frenzy, Burke caps it off with the collection, a lengthy process in which he all but hangs worshippers upside down to get their money. At the end of the service, the church has raised $1,070.90, a tidy sum from the 80-or-so smartly dressed people in this black, working-class neighbourhood.

It is another moment of magic in the life of Bishop Burke -- Solomon Burke, as he is known in the secular world, the "King of Rock and Soul." The latest venture for Burke, one of the biggest selling soul singers of the 1960s and a huge influence on many rock bands of the era, is an album entitled "The Definition of Soul" (Pointblank/Virgin). It reunites him with Jerry Wexler, the R&B producer who worked on Burke's greatest songs, and it features a duet with Little Richard.

He is famous for his involvement in an odd mix of business ventures over the years, most notably as a funeral director. Along the way, he found time to have 21 children (who have given him 45 grandchildren and three great-grandchildren so far), and they run the Burke businesses, including a half-dozen mortuaries, allowing him to focus on his twin loves of church and music.

"They won't let me embalm anymore because I'm old-time compared to the way they do things now," Burke, 61, told Reuters a few days before the service at the United House Of Prayer. So he has to be content as the spiritual leader of more than 172 churches worldwide.
"I've seen the miracles happen. I've seen things that are unbelievable happen through the power of prayer and believing. And that has kept me through my life on the right track."
Unlike Burke's late friend Sam Cooke, whom the gospel community never forgave when he crossed over to secular pop music, Burke found no difficulty straddling the two worlds.

Indeed the Philadelphia native complicated the equation in 1961 with his first hit, "Just Out of Reach (Of My Two Open Arms)," which happened to be a country song. Other hits followed including "Cry To Me," "If You Need Me," "Got To Get You Off My Mind" and "Tonight's The Night," all dripping with big emotion that spoke to the "heartland."

Burke toured relentlessly, establishing a reputation as an over-the-top performer complete with throne, an exact replica of Queen Elizabeth's Crown Jewels and regal velvets. He often toured as part of packages with the likes of Otis Redding and Joe Tex and he established a thriving business by selling food and drink on the bus to his parched comrades.

His 1964 song "Everybody Needs Somebody To Love" was covered by the Rolling Stones a year later. One of Burke's dreams is to perform it on stage with the Stones, whom he has never met but to whom he is most grateful for the royalties.

It used to nag Burke immensely that Wexler took a songwriting credit on that song. It was common practice in those days to share credits with people even if they didn't write the song. He once wrote Wexler a letter asking him to turn over his credit but never got a reply.
"I put away all these foolish things of hate and resentment and realised that for me to continue to survive I had to learn to love and forgive," he said.
Apparently swayed by Burke's new attitude, Wexler, now 80, last year emerged from retirement in Florida to produce the song "Your Time To Cry" on Burke's new album.

Burke was thrilled by that experience and awed by another: Little Richard turned up for a song that was finished by the time he arrived, so the flamboyant artist duetted in one take on "Everybody's Got A Game" with tears running down his cheeks while he sang.
Whether it's a humble church or a glitzy nightclub, Burke knows how to please an audience. "I'm blessed," he says. "I have to be the most blessed entertainer in the world."
